name: Whole wheat flour
what_it_is: Flour milled from the entire wheat kernel, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.
why_used: Provides structure and flavor in bread while retaining the bran and germ that refined flour removes.
evidence_summary: Whole grains as a food group are associated in human studies with higher fiber intake; this card describes the ingredient, not a health claim about any specific product.
practical_guidance: When it is the first grain listed, more of the grain content is whole grain, though the ingredient order alone does not give an exact percentage.
uncertainty: Ingredient order indicates relative quantity but not the precise whole-grain share of the product.

name: Enriched wheat flour
what_it_is: Refined wheat flour with the bran and germ removed, then enriched with specific B vitamins and iron.
why_used: Gives a soft, light crumb and consistent baking performance.
evidence_summary: Enrichment restores selected nutrients lost in refining; refined flour contains less fiber than whole grain flour.
practical_guidance: A product built mainly on enriched flour typically has less fiber than a comparable whole grain option.
uncertainty: Enrichment adds specific nutrients but does not replace the fiber of the whole grain.

name: Cane sugar
why_used: Adds sweetness, supports yeast fermentation, and contributes browning.
evidence_summary: Sugar added during processing counts as added sugar on the US label and is reported separately from naturally occurring total sugar.
practical_guidance: Compare the added sugar line at an equal weight rather than total sugar, which can include naturally present sugars.
uncertainty: Added sugar and total sugar are different measures and should not be substituted for one another.

name: Salt
what_it_is: Sodium chloride, the main dietary source of sodium.
why_used: Adds flavor, controls yeast activity, and acts as a preservative.
evidence_summary: Sodium content is reported in milligrams on the US label; this card does not assess any individual's sodium needs.
practical_guidance: Compare sodium at an equal weight across products in the same category.
uncertainty: Individual sodium targets vary; this is a general description, not personal dietary advice.

name: Whole grain oats
what_it_is: Oats that retain the bran, germ, and endosperm of the oat kernel.
why_used: Primary grain in many cereals; provides texture and a source of fiber.
evidence_summary: Oats are a whole grain; whole grains contribute dietary fiber, which this card describes at the ingredient level.
practical_guidance: When whole grain oats are the first ingredient, the product's grain base is predominantly whole grain.
uncertainty: The fiber contribution depends on the finished product's formulation and serving size.

name: Honey
what_it_is: A sweetener produced by bees, composed mainly of fructose and glucose.
evidence_summary: When added to a product, honey contributes to the added sugar total on the US label.
practical_guidance: Honey is still an added sugar for labeling purposes; compare the added sugar line at equal weight.
uncertainty: Marketing terms such as 'natural' do not change how added sugar is counted on the label.

name: Milled corn
what_it_is: Corn that has been milled, often with the germ removed, for use as a cereal grain base.
why_used: Forms the flake or grain base in many breakfast cereals.
evidence_summary: Degerminated milled corn is a refined grain and generally contributes less fiber than a whole grain base.
practical_guidance: A refined-corn base often pairs with a lower fiber figure; check the fiber line at equal weight.
uncertainty: Whether the corn is whole or refined depends on the specific product and is not always stated.

name: Rice
what_it_is: Milled rice used as the main grain in many crisp cereals; usually refined (bran and germ removed).
why_used: Gives a light, crisp texture as the grain base.
evidence_summary: Refined milled rice is not a whole grain and generally contributes little dietary fiber.
practical_guidance: A refined-rice base usually pairs with low fiber; check the fiber line at equal weight.
uncertainty: Some products use brown (whole grain) rice; the label states which.

name: Raisins
what_it_is: Dried grapes added to cereals for sweetness and texture.
why_used: Add natural sweetness, chew, and some fiber.
evidence_summary: Raisins contribute naturally occurring sugar (counted in total sugar) rather than added sugar, though many raisin cereals also add sugar separately.
practical_guidance: Total sugar can look high partly from the fruit; check the separate added sugar line.
uncertainty: Naturally occurring and added sugars are listed separately on the US label.

name: Malted barley flour
what_it_is: Flour from sprouted (malted) barley, used in small amounts for flavor and browning.
why_used: Adds a mild malt flavor and supports color and texture.
evidence_summary: Used in small quantities for flavor; not a major source of nutrients at those amounts. Contains gluten.
practical_guidance: A flavor ingredient, not a meaningful change to the fiber or sugar comparison.
uncertainty: Barley contains gluten, relevant for gluten avoidance.

name: Whole grain corn
what_it_is: Corn flour that retains the whole kernel, used as a whole-grain cereal base.
why_used: Provides the grain base while keeping the bran and germ.
evidence_summary: As a whole grain, it retains more fiber than degerminated milled corn, though a sweetened product can still be high in added sugar.
practical_guidance: Whole grain first is a plus, but still compare the added sugar line at equal weight.
uncertainty: Whole-grain base does not offset a high added-sugar formulation.
